<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:18pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:0%;font-style:italic;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"><a name="BROIN_II_CASES"></a><a name="BROIN_II_CASES"></a>Broin&#160;II Cases</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:6pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:4.54%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">RJR Tobacco, Lorillard Tobacco, B&amp;W and other cigarette manufacturer defendants settled <font style="font-style:italic;">Broin&#160;v. Philip Morris, Inc. </font>in October 1997. This case had been brought in Florida state court on behalf of flight attendants alleged to have suffered from diseases or ailments caused by exposure to ETS in airplane cabins. The settlement agreement required the participating tobacco companies to pay a total of $300&#160;million in three annual $100&#160;million installments, allocated among the companies by market share, to fund research on the early detection and cure of diseases associated with tobacco smoke. It also required those companies to pay a total of $49&#160;million for the plaintiffs&#8217; counsel&#8217;s fees and expenses. RJR Tobacco&#8217;s portion of these payments was approximately $86&#160;million; Lorillard Tobacco&#8217;s portion of these payments was approximately $57 million; and B&amp;W&#8217;s portion of these payments was approximately $31&#160;million. The settlement agreement bars class members from bringing aggregate claims or obtaining punitive damages and also bars individual claims to the extent that they are based on fraud, misrepresentation, conspiracy to commit fraud or misrepresentation, RICO, suppression, concealment or any other alleged intentional or willful conduct. The defendants agreed that, in any individual case brought by a class member, the defendant will bear the burden of proof with respect to whether ETS can cause certain specifically enumerated diseases, referred to as &#8220;general causation.&#8221; With respect to all other issues relating to liability, including whether an individual plaintiff&#8217;s disease was caused by his or her exposure to ETS in airplane cabins, referred to as &#8220;specific causation,&#8221; the individual plaintiff will have the burden of proof. On September&#160;7, 1999, the Florida Supreme Court approved the settlement. The <font style="font-style:italic;">Broin&#160;II </font>cases arose out of the settlement of this case.</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:4.54%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">On October&#160;5, 2000, the <font style="font-style:italic;">Broin </font>court entered an order applicable to all <font style="font-style:italic;">Broin&#160;II </font>cases that the terms of the <font style="font-style:italic;">Broin </font>settlement agreement do not require the individual <font style="font-style:italic;">Broin&#160;II </font>plaintiffs to prove the elements of strict liability, breach of warranty or negligence. </p>
<p style="text-align:center;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:0%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">129</p>
<hr style="page-break-after:always;width:100%;">
<p style="text-align:center;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;text-indent:0%;font-weight:bold;font-family:Times New Roman Bold;font-size:10pt;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"><font style="Background-color:#FFFFFF;">NOTES TO CONSOLIDATED FINANCIAL STATEMENTS &#8212; continued</font></p>
<p style="margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;text-indent:0%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">&#160;</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">Under this order, there is a </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">rebuttable presumption in the plaintiffs&#8217; favor on those elements, and the plaintiffs bear the burden of proving that their alleged adverse health effects actually were caused by exposure to ETS in airplane cabins, that is, specific causation.</font></p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:4.54%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">As of December 31, 2015, there were 2,499 <font style="font-style:italic;">Broin II</font> lawsuits pending in Florida. There have been no <font style="font-style:italic;">Broin II</font> trials since 2007.</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:18pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:0%;font-style:italic;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"><a name="CLASSACTION_SUITS"></a><a name="CLASSACTION_SUITS"></a>Class-Action Suits</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:6pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:4.54%;font-style:italic;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">Overview.<font style="font-style:normal;"> As of December 31, 2015, 16 class-action cases, excluding the shareholder cases described below, were pending in the United States against Reynolds Defendants. These class actions seek recovery for personal injuries allegedly caused by cigarette smoking or, in some cases, for economic damages allegedly incurred by cigarette or e-cigarette purchasers. </font></p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:4.54%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">In 1996, the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals in <font style="font-style:italic;">Castano&#160;v. American Tobacco Co.</font> overturned the certification of a nation-wide class of persons whose claims related to alleged addiction to tobacco products. Since this ruling by the Fifth Circuit, most class-action suits have sought certification of state-wide, rather than nation-wide, classes. Class-action suits based on claims similar to those asserted in <font style="font-style:italic;">Castano,</font> claims that class members are at a greater risk of injury or injured by the use of tobacco or exposure to ETS, or claims that seek primarily economic damages are pending against RJR Tobacco, Lorillard Tobacco, or their affiliates or indemnitees in state or federal courts in Illinois, Louisiana, Missouri, West Virginia, California, Florida, New York and New Mexico. All pending class-action cases are discussed below.</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:4.54%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">The pending class actions against RJR Tobacco or its affiliates or indemnitees include four cases alleging that the use of the term &#8220;lights&#8221; constitutes unfair and deceptive trade practices under state law or violates the federal RICO statute. Such suits are pending in state or federal courts in Illinois and Missouri and are discussed below under &#8220;&#8212;&#160;&#8216;Lights&#8217; Cases.&#8221;</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:4.54%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">E-cigarette class-action cases are pending against RJR Vapor, RAI, and other RAI affiliates in California. In general, the plaintiffs allege that RJR Vapor, Lorillard Tobacco, and other RAI affiliates made false and misleading claims that e-cigarettes are less hazardous than other cigarette products or failed to disclose that e-cigarettes expose users to certain substances. The cases are typically filed pursuant to state consumer protection and related statutes and seek recovery of economic damages.</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:4.54%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">Several class actions relating to claims in advertising and promotional materials for SFNTC&#8217;s NATURAL AMERICAN SPIRIT brand cigarettes are pending in federal courts. In general, these plaintiffs allege that use of the words &#8220;natural,&#8221; &#8220;additive-free,&#8221; or &#8220;organic&#8221; in NATURAL AMERICAN SPIRIT advertising and promotional materials suggests that those cigarettes are less harmful than other cigarettes and, for that reason, violated state consumer protection statutes or amounted to fraud or a negligent or intentional misrepresentation. The cases seek various combinations of recovery, including economic damages, treble damages, statutory damages, punitive damages, injunctive relief (including medical monitoring), and attorneys&#8217; fees, costs and expenses.</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:4.54%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">Finally, certain third-party payers have filed health-care cost recovery actions in the form of class actions. These cases are discussed below under &#8220;&#8212;&#160;Health-Care Cost Recovery Cases.&#8221;</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:4.54%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">Few smoker class-action complaints have been certified or, if certified, have survived on appeal. Eighteen federal courts, including two courts of appeals, and most state courts that have considered the issue have rejected class certification in such cases. Apart from the <font style="font-style:italic;">Castano </font>case discussed above, only two smoker class actions have been certified by a federal court&#160;&#8212; <font style="font-style:italic;">In re Simon (II)&#160;Litigation,</font> and <font style="font-style:italic;">Schwab [McLaughlin]&#160;v. Philip Morris USA, Inc.</font>, both of which were filed in the U.S.&#160;District Court for the Eastern District of New York and were ultimately decertified.</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:4.54%;font-style:italic;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">Camel Cash Cases. Sateriale v.&#160;R. J. Reynolds Tobacco Co.<font style="font-style:normal;">, is a class action filed in November 2009 in the U.S.&#160;District Court for the Central District of California relating to the termination of a series of promotions by RJR Tobacco&#8217;s CAMEL brand from 1991 to 2007 known as &#8220;Camel Cash.&#8221; The plaintiffs originally brought the case on behalf of a putative class of all persons who tried unsuccessfully to redeem Camel Cash certificates from October 1, 1991 through March&#160;31, 2007, or who held Camel Cash certificates as of March&#160;31, 2007. The plaintiffs alleged that RJR Tobacco failed to have any rewards available during the final promotional period. The plaintiffs alleged claims based on the California Unfair Competition Law, the California Consumer Legal Remedies Law, breach of contract and promissory estoppel, and the plaintiffs sought injunctive relief, actual damages, costs and expenses. In January&#160;2010, RJR Tobacco filed a motion to dismiss. In February 2010, the plaintiffs filed an amended complaint. In the amended complaint, the proposed class definition changed to a class consisting of all persons who reside in the U.S. and tried unsuccessfully to redeem Camel Cash certificates, also referred to as C-Notes, from October 1, 2006 to March 31, 2007. The plaintiffs also proposed a California subclass consisting of persons in California meeting the same criteria. In May 2010, RJR Tobacco&#8217;s motion to dismiss the amended complaint for lack of subject matter jurisdiction and, alternatively, for failure to state a claim was granted with leave to amend. The plaintiffs filed a second amended complaint. In July 2010, RJR Tobacco&#8217;s motion to dismiss the second amended complaint was granted with leave to amend. The plaintiffs filed a third amended complaint, and RJR Tobacco filed a motion to </font></p>
<p style="text-align:center;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:0%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">130</p>
<hr style="page-break-after:always;width:100%;">
<p style="text-align:center;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;text-indent:0%;font-weight:bold;font-family:Times New Roman Bold;font-size:10pt;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"><font style="Background-color:#FFFFFF;">NOTES TO CONSOLIDATED FINANCIAL STATEMENTS &#8212; continued</font></p>
<p style="margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;text-indent:0%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">&#160;</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;font-style:italic;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"><font style="font-style:normal;">dismiss in September 2010. In December 2010, the</font><font style="font-style:normal;"> district</font><font style="font-style:normal;"> court granted RJR Tobacco&#8217;s </font><font style="font-style:normal;">motion to dismiss with prejudice</font><font style="font-style:normal;"> and</font><font style="font-style:normal;"> entered </font><font style="font-style:normal;">final judgment. In January 2011,</font><font style="font-style:normal;"> the plaintiffs filed a notice of appeal</font><font style="font-style:normal;">. </font><font style="font-style:normal;">In July 2012, the </font><font style="font-style:normal;">U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, referred to as the Ninth Circuit,</font><font style="font-style:normal;"> affirmed the dismissal of the plaintiffs</font><font style="font-style:normal;">&#8217; claims under the </font><font style="font-style:normal;">California </font><font style="font-style:normal;">Unfair Competition Law and the</font><font style="font-style:normal;"> California</font><font style="font-style:normal;"> Consumer Legal Remedies Acts and reversed the dismissal of the plaintiffs&#8217; claims for promissory estoppel and breach of contract. </font><font style="font-style:normal;">In October 2012, the Ninth Circuit denied </font><font style="font-style:normal;">RJR Tobacco&#8217;</font><font style="font-style:normal;">s motion for rehearing or rehearing </font><font style="font-style:italic;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">en banc</font><font style="font-style:normal;">. </font><font style="font-style:normal;">RJR Tobacco filed its answer to the plaintiffs&#8217; third amended complaint in December 2012. </font><font style="font-style:normal;">Following the completion of discovery in</font><font style="font-style:normal;"> June 2014, RJR Tobacco filed a motion for summary judgment, and the </font><font style="font-style:normal;">plaintiffs</font><font style="font-style:normal;"> f</font><font style="font-style:normal;">iled a motion for class certification. On December</font><font style="font-style:normal;"> </font><font style="font-style:normal;">19, 2014, the </font><font style="font-style:normal;">district </font><font style="font-style:normal;">court </font><font style="font-style:normal;">denied RJR Tobacco&#8217;s motion for summary judgment, declined to certify a national class, found that the plaintiffs&#8217; promissory estoppel claim could not be tried on a class basis</font><font style="font-style:normal;">, and, on the plaintiffs&#8217; breach of contract claim, </font><font style="font-style:normal;">certified a class of </font><font style="font-style:normal;">&#8220;all persons in </font><font style="font-style:normal;">California who</font><font style="font-style:normal;">, as adult smokers, were assigned registration numbers by RJR Tobacco, collected C-Notes, and held C-Notes as of</font><font style="font-style:normal;"> October</font><font style="font-style:normal;"> </font><font style="font-style:normal;">1, 2006</font><font style="font-style:normal;">.&#8221; RJR Tobacco filed a mo</font><font style="font-style:normal;">tion to decertify the class and further discovery was stayed. Subsequently, the parties agreed to a settlement. Pursuant to the proposed settlement, RJR Tobacco would make available non-tobacco merchandise to class members for Camel Cash that they held on </font><font style="font-style:normal;">October 1, 2006, and pay plaintiffs&#8217; counsel $4.75 million in fees and costs. </font><font style="font-style:normal;">On January 19, 2016, the court granted its preliminary approval order for the settlement. A fairness hearing will be held by the court on May 2, 2016. </font></p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:4.54%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">In <font style="font-style:italic;">Feinman v. R. J. Reynolds Tobacco Co.</font>, a putative class action filed in September 2015, in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York, the plaintiff brought a case against RJR Tobacco on behalf of a putative class of residents of New York, Iowa and South Dakota who were excluded from the California class in <font style="font-style:italic;">Sateriale</font>; namely, all persons who resided in New York, Iowa or South Dakota as of October 1, 2006, and who, as adult smokers, purchased Camel-brand filtered cigarettes along with C-Notes, collected C-Notes and held C-Notes as of October 1, 2006. The plaintiff alleges breach of contract claims based on the termination of a series of promotions by RJR Tobacco&#8217;s Camel brand from 1991 to 2007 known as &#8220;Camel Cash.&#8221; On September 28, 2015, RJR Tobacco accepted service of process of the complaint. On January 16, 2016, the court conditionally approved the parties&#8217; settlement agreement and dismissal of the case subject to the court in <font style="font-style:italic;">Sateriale</font> granting its final approval of that settlement agreement.</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:4.54%;font-style:italic;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">E-Cigarette Cases<font style="font-style:normal;">. In </font>Diek v. Lorillard Tobacco Co., <font style="font-style:normal;">a putative class action filed in April 2015, in the Superior Court of California, Orange County, the plaintiff brought a case against Lorillard Tobacco and two affiliated entities on behalf of a putative class of purchasers of one or more blu brand e-cigarettes, including e-juices, components thereof, cartridges or accessories sold by the defendants. The plaintiff alleges that certain advertising, marketing and packaging materials for blu brand e-cigarettes made deceptive claims and omitted material information. The plaintiff seeks injunctive relief under California Civil Code &#167;1,750 </font>et seq<font style="font-style:normal;">., injunctive and equitable relief under California Business &amp; Professions Code &#167;17,200 </font>et seq<font style="font-style:normal;">., injunctive relief and damages under California Business and Professions Code &#167;17,500 </font>et seq<font style="font-style:normal;">., and damages for purported breaches of express warranty. On June 18, 2015, pursuant to the terms of the Asset Purchase Agreement, RAI tendered the defense of this action to, and sought indemnification for this action from, Imperial Sub. On June 26, 2015, the defendants removed the action to the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California. On October 2, 2015, the plaintiffs filed an amended complaint naming as defendants RAI, two RAI affiliates, Imperial Sub, and two Imperial Sub affiliates. Pursuant to the terms and conditions of the Asset Purchase Agreement, Imperial Sub has agreed to defend and indemnify RAI and its affiliates.</font></p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:4.54%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">In <font style="font-style:italic;">Whitney v. ITG Brands, LLC</font>, a putative class action filed in September 2015, in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, the plaintiff brought a case against RAI, an RAI affiliate, Imperial Sub, and an Imperial Sub affiliate on behalf of a putative class of purchasers of blu brand e-cigarettes. The plaintiff alleges that certain advertising, marketing and packaging materials for blu brand e-cigarettes failed to advise purchasers and users that they potentially could be exposed to formaldehyde. The plaintiff asserts claims under California Business &amp; Professions Code &#167;17,200 <font style="font-style:italic;">et seq.</font> and California Civil Code &#167;1,750 <font style="font-style:italic;">et seq</font>. and seeks declaratory relief, restitution, disgorgement, injunctive relief and damages. On September 18, 2015, pursuant to the terms of the Asset Purchase Agreement, RAI tendered the defense of this action to, and sought indemnification for this action from, Imperial Sub. Pursuant to the terms and conditions of the Asset Purchase Agreement, Imperial Sub has agreed to defend and indemnify RAI and its affiliate.</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:4.54%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">In <font style="font-style:italic;">Harris v. R. J. Reynolds Vapor Co.</font>, a putative class action filed in September 2015, in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, the plaintiff brought a case against RJR Vapor on behalf of a putative class of purchasers of VUSE e-cigarettes. The plaintiff alleges that certain advertising, marketing and packaging materials for VUSE e-cigarettes failed to advise purchasers and users that they potentially could be exposed to formaldehyde and acetaldehyde. The plaintiff asserts claim under California Business &amp; Professions Code &#167; 17,200 <font style="font-style:italic;">et seq</font>. and California Civil Code &#167; 1,750 <font style="font-style:italic;">et seq</font>. and seeks declaratory relief, restitution, disgorgement, injunctive relief and damages. RJR Vapor accepted service of process on September 23, 2015. An amended complaint was subsequently filed alleging a violation of Proposition 65. RJR Vapor filed a motion to dismiss on January 8, 2016. A decision is pending.</p>
<p style="text-align:center;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:0%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">131</p>
<hr style="page-break-after:always;width:100%;">
<p style="text-align:center;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;text-indent:0%;font-weight:bold;font-family:Times New Roman Bold;font-size:10pt;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"><font style="Background-color:#FFFFFF;">NOTES TO CONSOLIDATED FINANCIAL STATEMENTS &#8212; continued</font></p>
<p style="margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;text-indent:0%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">&#160;</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:4.54%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">In </font><font style="font-style:italic;">Center for Environmental Health v. NJoy, Inc.</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">, on November 19, 2015, the Center for Environmental Hea</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">lth filed a complaint in the Superior Court, Alameda County, California against RJR Vapor and several other e-cigarette manufacturers asserting a violation of Proposition 65 for not disclosing that electronic cigarettes, including VUSE, allegedly expose co</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">nsumers to formaldehyde and acetaldehyde. RJR Vapor filed an answer on December 29, 2015.</font></p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:4.54%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">&#8220;<font style="font-style:italic;">Lights</font>&#8221; <font style="font-style:italic;">Cases</font>. As noted above, &#8220;lights&#8221; class-action cases are pending against RJR Tobacco or B&amp;W in Illinois (2) and Missouri (2). The classes in these cases generally seek to recover $50,000 to $75,000 per class member for compensatory and punitive damages, injunctive and other forms of relief, and attorneys&#8217; fees and costs from RJR Tobacco and/or B&amp;W. In general, the plaintiffs allege that RJR Tobacco or B&amp;W made false and misleading claims that &#8220;lights&#8221; cigarettes were lower in tar and nicotine and/or were less hazardous or less mutagenic than other cigarettes. The cases typically are filed pursuant to state consumer protection and related statutes.</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:4.54%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">Many of these &#8220;lights&#8221; cases were stayed pending review of the <font style="font-style:italic;">Good&#160;v. Altria Group, Inc</font>. case by the U.S.&#160;Supreme Court. In that &#8220;lights&#8221; class-action case against Altria Group, Inc. and Philip Morris USA Inc., the U.S.&#160;Supreme Court decided that these claims are not preempted by the Federal Cigarette Labeling and Advertising Act or by the Federal Trade Commission&#8217;s, referred to as FTC, historic regulation of the industry. Since this decision in December 2008, a number of the stayed cases have become active again.</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:4.54%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">The seminal &#8220;lights&#8221; class-action case involves RJR Tobacco&#8217;s competitor, Philip Morris, Inc. Trial began in <font style="font-style:italic;">Price&#160;v. Philip Morris, Inc</font>. in January 2003. In March 2003, the trial judge entered judgment against Philip Morris in the amount of $7.1&#160;billion in compensatory damages and $3&#160;billion in punitive damages. Based on Illinois law, the bond required to stay execution of the judgment was set initially at $12&#160;billion. Philip Morris pursued various avenues of relief from the $12&#160;billion bond requirement. On December 15, 2005, the Illinois Supreme Court reversed the lower court&#8217;s decision and sent the case back to the trial court with instructions to dismiss the case. On December 5, 2006, the trial court granted the defendant&#8217;s motion to dismiss and for entry of final judgment. The case was dismissed with prejudice the same day. In December&#160;2008, the plaintiffs filed a petition for relief from judgment, stating that the U.S.&#160;Supreme Court&#8217;s decision in <font style="font-style:italic;">Good&#160;v. Altria Group, Inc</font>. rejected the basis for the reversal. The trial court granted the defendant&#8217;s motion to dismiss the plaintiffs&#8217; petition for relief from judgment in February&#160;2009. In March&#160;2009, the plaintiffs filed a notice of appeal to the Illinois Appellate Court, Fifth Judicial District, requesting a reversal of the February&#160;2009 order and remand to the circuit court. On February<font style="color:#000000;"> </font>24, 2011, the appellate court entered an order, concluding that the two-year time limit for filing a petition for relief from a final judgment began to run when the trial court dismissed the plaintiffs&#8217; lawsuit on December<font style="color:#000000;"> </font>18, 2006.<font style="color:#000000;"> </font>The appellate court therefore found that the petition was timely, reversed the order of the trial court, and remanded the case for further proceedings. Philip Morris filed a petition for leave to appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court. On September<font style="color:#000000;"> </font>28, 2011, the Illinois Supreme Court denied Philip Morris&#8217;s petition for leave to appeal and returned the case to the trial court for further proceedings. In December 2012, the trial court denied the plaintiffs&#8217; petition for relief from the judgment.<font style="color:#000000;"> </font>The plaintiffs filed a notice of appeal to the Illinois Appellate Court, Fifth Judicial District. In April 2014, the appellate court reinstated the 2003 verdict. In May 2014, Philip Morris filed a petition for leave to appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court and a motion for supervisory order. Philip Morris has requested the Illinois Supreme Court to direct the Fifth Judicial District to vacate its April 2014 judgment and to order the Fifth Judicial District to affirm the trial court&#8217;s denial of the plaintiff&#8217;s petition for relief from the judgment, or in the alternative, grant its petition for leave to appeal. On September<font style="color:#000000;"> </font>24, 2014, the Illinois Supreme Court agreed to hear Philip Morris&#8217;s appeal. <font style="color:#000000;">In November 2015, the Illinois Supreme Court vacated the judgments of the lower courts and dismissed the case without prejudice to allow the plaintiffs to file a motion to recall the mandate. The plaintiffs filed a motion to recall the mandate or for other appropriate relief in the Illinois Supreme Court, which was denied on January 11, 2016.</font></p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:4.54%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">In <font style="font-style:italic;">Turner v.&#160;R. J. Reynolds Tobacco Co., </font>a case filed in February 2000, in Circuit Court, Madison County, Illinois, a judge certified a class in November&#160;2001. In November&#160;2003, the Illinois Supreme Court granted RJR Tobacco&#8217;s motion for a stay pending the court&#8217;s final appeal decision in the <font style="font-style:italic;">Price </font>case mentioned above<font style="font-style:italic;">. </font>The stay subsequently expired, and the court accordingly scheduled a series of status conferences, all of which were continued by agreement of the parties. The next status conference is scheduled for February 24, 2016.</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:4.54%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">In <font style="font-style:italic;">Howard v.&#160;Brown&#160;&amp; Williamson Tobacco Corp., </font>another case filed in February 2000 in Circuit Court, Madison County, Illinois, a judge certified a class in December&#160;2001. In June&#160;2003, the trial judge issued an order staying all proceedings pending resolution of the <font style="font-style:italic;">Price&#160;</font>case mentioned above. The plaintiffs appealed this stay order to the Illinois Fifth District Court of Appeals, which affirmed the Circuit Court&#8217;s stay order in August&#160;2005. There is currently no activity in the case.</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:4.54%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">A &#8220;lights&#8221; class-action case is pending against each of RJR Tobacco and B&amp;W in Missouri. In <font style="font-style:italic;">Collora&#160;v. R. J. Reynolds Tobacco Co., </font>a case filed in May 2000 in Circuit Court, St.&#160;Louis County, Missouri, a judge in St.&#160;Louis certified a class in December&#160;2003. In April&#160;2007, the court granted the plaintiffs&#8217; motion to reassign <font style="font-style:italic;">Collora </font>and the following cases to a single general division: <font style="font-style:italic;">Craft&#160;v. Philip Morris USA Inc. </font>and <font style="font-style:italic;">Black&#160;v. Brown&#160;&amp; Williamson Tobacco Corp., </font>discussed below. In April&#160;2008, the court </p>
<p style="text-align:center;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:0%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">132</p>
<hr style="page-break-after:always;width:100%;">
<p style="text-align:center;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;text-indent:0%;font-weight:bold;font-family:Times New Roman Bold;font-size:10pt;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"><font style="Background-color:#FFFFFF;">NOTES TO CONSOLIDATED FINANCIAL STATEMENTS &#8212; continued</font></p>
<p style="margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;text-indent:0%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">&#160;</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">stayed the case pending U.S.&#160;Supreme</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"> Court review in </font><font style="font-style:italic;">Good&#160;v. Altria Group, Inc</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">. </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">A nominal trial date of January 10, 2011 was scheduled, but it did not proceed at that time. </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">A status conference is scheduled for February 22, 2016.</font></p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:4.54%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">Finally, in <font style="font-style:italic;">Black v.&#160;Brown&#160;&amp; Williamson Tobacco Corp., </font>a case filed in November 2000 in Circuit Court, City of St.&#160;Louis, Missouri, the trial court, in April 2008, stayed the case pending U.S.&#160;Supreme Court review in <font style="font-style:italic;">Good&#160;v. Altria Group, Inc. </font>A nominal trial date of January 10, 2011, was scheduled, but it did not proceed at that time. A status conference is scheduled for February 22, 2016.</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:4.54%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">In the event RJR Tobacco and its affiliates or indemnitees lose one or more of the pending &#8220;lights&#8221; class-action suits, RJR Tobacco, depending upon the amount of any damages ordered, could face difficulties in its ability to pay the judgment or obtain any bond required to stay execution of the judgment which could have a material adverse effect on RJR Tobacco&#8217;s, and consequently RAI&#8217;s, results of operations, cash flows or financial position.</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:4.54%;font-style:italic;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">No Additive/Natural Claim Cases<font style="font-style:normal;">. Following the FDA&#8217;s August 27, 2015, warning letter to SFNTC relating to the use of the words &#8220;natural&#8221; and &#8220;additive-free&#8221; in the labeling, advertising, and promotional materials for NATURAL AMERICAN SPIRIT brand cigarettes, plaintiffs purporting to bring claims on behalf of themselves and others have filed putative class actions against SFNTC and RAI. There are currently a total of seven such actions that are pending in the U.S. district courts for the Southern and Middle Districts of Florida, Southern District of New York, District of New Mexico, and Northern District of California. The claims asserted in these actions are based on alleged violations of state deceptive and unfair trade practice statutes, state common law, fraud, negligent misrepresentation, and unjust enrichment, and the cases seek various combinations of recovery, including economic damages, injunctive relief, interest, restitution, disgorgement, treble and punitive damages, and attorneys&#8217; fees and costs. On January 6, 2016, the plaintiffs in one of these actions filed a motion before the U.S. Judicial Panel On Multidistrict Litigation to consolidate these actions, referred to as the MDL Motion. SFNTC and RAI responded to the motion on January 27, 2016, and the hearing before the Judicial Panel On Multidistrict Litigation is anticipated on the Panel&#8217;s March 31, 2016 or May 26, 2016 hearing dates.</font><font style="border-bottom:double 2.5pt #0000FF;color:#0000FF;font-style:normal;"> </font></p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:4.54%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">In <font style="font-style:italic;">Sproule v. Santa Fe Natural Tobacco Co.</font>, a putative class action filed in September 2015, in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida, the plaintiff brought a case against SFNTC and RAI on behalf of a nationwide putative class of purchasers of <font style="text-transform:uppercase;">Natural American Spirit </font>brand cigarettes. The plaintiff alleges that use of the words &#8220;natural,&#8221; &#8220;additive-free,&#8221; &#8220;organic,&#8221; and &#8220;unadulterated tobacco product,&#8221; suggests that <font style="text-transform:uppercase;">Natural American Spirit</font> brand cigarettes are healthier than or present reduced health risks as compared to other cigarettes. The plaintiff asserts claims based on alleged violations of the Florida Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act, as well as claims for fraud, negligent misrepresentation, unjust enrichment, and, as to RAI, for aiding and abetting and vicarious liability. The plaintiff seeks injunctive relief, including medical monitoring and smoking cessation programs, compensatory damages, civil penalties and statutory damages, prejudgment and post-judgment interest, attorneys&#8217; fees and punitive damages. The defendants filed a motion to dismiss on December 15, 2015. On January 26, 2016, the <font style="font-style:italic;">Sproule</font> court stayed all proceedings pending resolution of the MDL Motion.</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:4.54%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">In <font style="font-style:italic;">Brattain v. Santa Fe Natural Tobacco Co., </font>a putative class action filed in October 2015, in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, the plaintiff brought the case against SFNTC and RAI on behalf of a putative class of California purchasers of <font style="text-transform:uppercase;">Natural American Spirit</font> brand cigarettes. The plaintiff alleges that use of the words &#8220;natural,&#8221; &#8220;100% additive free,&#8221; and &#8220;organic&#8221; suggests that <font style="text-transform:uppercase;">Natural American Spirit</font> brand cigarettes are healthier than or present reduced health risks as compared to other cigarettes. The plaintiff asserts claims based on alleged violations of the California Business &amp; Professions Code &#167; 17,500 <font style="font-style:italic;">et seq</font>., California Business &amp; Professions Code &#167; 17,200 <font style="font-style:italic;">et seq</font>. and California Civil Code &#167; 1,750 <font style="font-style:italic;">et seq</font>., and seeks injunctive relief, restitution, disgorgement, compensatory damages, attorneys&#8217; fees, costs and prejudgment and post-judgment interest. The defendants filed a motion to dismiss on December 14, 2015. On January 22, 2016, the <font style="font-style:italic;">Brattain</font> court stayed all proceedings pending resolution of the MDL Motion. </p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:4.54%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"><a name="_cp_text_1_80"></a><a name="_cp_text_1_81"></a>In <font style="font-style:italic;"><a name="_cp_text_1_81"></a>Rothman v. Santa Fe Natural Tobacco Co.</font>, a putative class action filed in November 2015, in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York, the plaintiff brought a case against SFNTC and RAI on behalf of a putative class of New York purchasers of NATURAL AMERICAN SPIRIT brand cigarettes. The plaintiff alleges that the use of the words &#8220;natural&#8221; and &#8220;additive-free&#8221; suggest that NATURAL AMERICAN SPIRIT brand cigarettes present a lower risk of tobacco-related disease and are less harmful than other commercially available cigarettes. The plaintiff asserts claims based on alleged violations of New York General Business Law &#167;&#167;&#160;349-50 and a claim for unjust enrichment. The plaintiff seeks injunctive relief, compensatory damages, statutory damages, restitution, and attorneys&#8217; fees and expenses. The defendants have not yet filed their initial response. On January 25, 2016, the parties jointly requested a stay of all proceedings pending resolution of the MDL Motion. </p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:4.54%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"><a name="_cp_text_1_83"></a><a name="_cp_text_1_84"></a>In <font style="font-style:italic;"><a name="_cp_text_1_84"></a>Dunn v. Santa Fe Natural Tobacco Co.</font>, a putative class action filed in December 2015, in the U.S. District Court for the District of New Mexico, the plaintiff brought a case against SFNTC on behalf of a nationwide putative class (and Minnesota subclass) of purchasers of NATURAL AMERICAN SPIRIT brand cigarettes. The plaintiff alleges that the use of the word &#8220;natural&#8221; suggests </p>
<p style="text-align:center;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:0%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">133</p>
<hr style="page-break-after:always;width:100%;">
<p style="text-align:center;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;text-indent:0%;font-weight:bold;font-family:Times New Roman Bold;font-size:10pt;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"><font style="Background-color:#FFFFFF;">NOTES TO CONSOLIDATED FINANCIAL STATEMENTS &#8212; continued</font></p>
<p style="margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;text-indent:0%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">&#160;</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">that NATURAL AMERICAN SPIRIT brand cigarettes are less harmful than other commercially available cigarettes. The plaintiff asserts claims based on alleged violations of the Minnesota Consumer Fraud Act, Min</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">nesota Unlawful Trade Practices Act, Minnesota Deceptive Trade Practices Act, Minnesota False Advertising Law, and New Mexico Unfair Trade Practices Act, negligent misrepresentation, and unjust enrichment. The plaintiff seeks compensatory, treble, and puni</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">tive damages, restitution, disgorgement, injunctive relief, and attorneys&#8217; fees and costs. The defendants have not yet filed their initial response.</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"> On February 1, 2016, the parties filed a joint motion to stay all proceedings pending resolution of the MDL</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"> Motion.</font></p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:4.54%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"><a name="_cp_text_1_86"></a><a name="_cp_text_1_87"></a>In <font style="font-style:italic;"><a name="_cp_text_1_87"></a>Haksal v. Santa Fe Natural Tobacco Co.</font>, a putative class action filed in December 2015, in the U.S. District Court for the District of New Mexico, the plaintiffs brought a case against SFNTC and RAI on behalf of a nationwide putative class (and California, Illinois, Minnesota, and New Mexico subclasses) of purchasers of NATURAL AMERICAN SPIRIT brand cigarettes. The plaintiffs allege that the use of the words &#8220;natural,&#8221; &#8220;additive-free,&#8221; and &#8220;organic&#8221; and the use of Native American imagery, suggests that NATURAL AMERICAN SPIRIT brand cigarettes are less harmful than other commercially available cigarettes. The plaintiffs further challenge use of the description &#8220;natural&#8221; based on alleged use of artificial fertilizers and tobacco produced from genetically modified organism (GMO) tobacco, and allege false and misleading environmental claims. The plaintiffs assert claims based on alleged violations of the New Mexico Unfair Practices Act, New Mexico False Advertising Act, California Unfair Competition Law, California False Advertising Law, Minnesota Uniform Deceptive Trade Practices Act, Minnesota Prevention of Consumer Fraud Act, Minnesota False Statement in Advertising Act, Illinois Consumer Fraud and Deceptive Business Practices Act, and Illinois Uniform Deceptive Trade Practices Act, fraud, intentional misrepresentation, deceit, negligent misrepresentation, quasi-contract, and unjust enrichment. The plaintiffs seek compensatory exemplary, treble, and punitive damages, restitution, disgorgement, attorneys&#8217; fees and costs, and injunctive relief, including recall of allegedly unlawfully labeled product. The defendants have not yet filed their initial response. On February 1, 2016, the parties filed a joint motion to stay all proceedings pending resolution of the MDL Motion.</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:4.54%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"><a name="_cp_text_1_88"></a>In <font style="font-style:italic;">Cuebas v. Santa Fe Natural Tobacco Co.</font>, a putative class action filed in January 2016, in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York, the plaintiff brought a case against SFNTC and RAI on behalf of a nationwide putative class (and New York subclass) of purchasers of NATURAL AMERICAN SPIRIT brand cigarettes. The plaintiff alleges that the use of the words &#8220;natural,&#8221; &#8220;additive-free,&#8221; &#8220;100% additive free,&#8221; &#8220;organic,&#8221; and &#8220;unadulterated tobacco product&#8221; suggest that NATURAL AMERICAN SPIRIT brand cigarettes are less harmful than other commercially available cigarettes. The plaintiff asserts claims based on alleged violations of New York General Business Law &#167;&#167;&#160;349-50, fraud, negligent misrepresentation, and unjust enrichment. The plaintiff seeks compensatory, treble and exemplary damages, civil penalties, injunctive relief including medical monitoring and smoking cessation programs, interest, attorneys&#8217; fees, costs, and punitive damages. The defendants have not yet filed their initial response.</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:4.54%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">In <font style="font-style:italic;">Okstad v. Santa Fe Natural Tobacco Co.</font>, a putative class action filed in January 2016, in the U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Florida, the plaintiffs brought a case against SFNTC and RAI on behalf of a nationwide putative class and sixteen putative state-based subclasses (Alabama, California, Colorado, Florida, Georgia, Iowa, Illinois, Maryland, Maine, North Carolina, New Jersey, Ohio, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Texas and Wisconsin subclasses) of purchasers of NATURAL AMERICAN SPIRIT brand cigarettes. The plaintiffs allege that the use of the words &#8220;natural,&#8221; &#8220;additive free,&#8221; &#8220;100% additive free,&#8221; &#8220;organic,&#8221; and &#8220;unadulterated tobacco product&#8221; suggests that NATURAL AMERICAN SPIRIT brand cigarettes are less harmful than other commercially available cigarettes. On behalf of the putative nationwide class, plaintiffs assert common law claims of alleged fraud, negligent misrepresentation, and unjust enrichment. On behalf of the 16 state-based subclasses, plaintiffs assert claims based on alleged violations of the Alabama Deceptive Trade Practice Act, California Consumers Legal Remedies Act, California False Advertising Law, Colorado Consumer Protection Act, Georgia&#8217;s Fair Business Practices Act, Georgia&#8217;s Uniform Deceptive Trade Practices Act, Illinois Consumer Fraud and Deceptive Business Practices Act, Iowa Private Right of Action for Consumer Frauds Act, Maine Unfair Trade Practices Act, Maryland Consumer Protection Act, New Jersey Consumer Fraud Act, North Carolina Unfair and Deceptive Trade Practices Act, Ohio Consumer Sales Practices Act, Oregon Unlawful Trade Practices Act, Pennsylvania Unfair Trade Practices and Consumer Protection Law, Texas Deceptive Trade Practices Act, and Wisconsin Deceptive Trade Practices Act. The plaintiffs seek compensatory, treble, and exemplary damages, injunctive relief, including medical monitoring and smoking cessation programs, civil penalties, interest, attorneys&#8217; fees, costs, and punitive damages. The defendants have not yet filed their initial response. </p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:4.54%;font-style:italic;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">Other Class&#160;Actions. <font style="font-style:normal;">In</font> Young&#160;v. American Tobacco Co., Inc., <font style="font-style:normal;">a case filed in November 1997 in Circuit Court, Orleans Parish, Louisiana, the plaintiffs brought an ETS class action against U.S.&#160;cigarette manufacturers, including RJR Tobacco and B&amp;W, and parent companies of U.S.&#160;cigarette manufacturers, including RJR, on behalf of all residents of Louisiana who, though not themselves cigarette smokers, have been exposed to secondhand smoke from cigarettes which were manufactured by the defendants, and who allegedly suffered injury as a result of that exposure. The plaintiffs seek to recover an unspecified amount of compensatory and punitive damages.  In March 2013, the court entered an order staying the case, including all discovery, pending the implementation of the smoking cessation program ordered by the court in </font>Scott v. The American Tobacco Co<font style="font-style:normal;">.</font></p>
<p style="text-align:center;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:0%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">134</p>
<hr style="page-break-after:always;width:100%;">
<p style="text-align:center;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;text-indent:0%;font-weight:bold;font-family:Times New Roman Bold;font-size:10pt;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"><font style="Background-color:#FFFFFF;">NOTES TO CONSOLIDATED FINANCIAL STATEMENTS &#8212; continued</font></p>
<p style="margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;text-indent:0%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">&#160;</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:4.54%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">In </font><font style="font-style:italic;">Parsons v.&#160;A C&#160;&amp; S, Inc., </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">a case filed in February 1998 in Circuit Court, Ohio County, West Virginia, the plaintiff sued asbestos manufacturers, </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">U.S.&#160;cigarette manufacturers, including RJR Tobacco</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">,</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"> B&amp;W</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">, Lorillard Tobacco</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">, and parent companies of U.S.&#160;cigarette manufacturers, including RJR</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"> and Lorillard</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">, seeking to recover $1&#160;million in compensatory and punitive damages individually and an unspecifi</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">ed amount for the class in both compensatory and punitive damages. The case was brought on behalf of persons who allegedly have personal injury claims arising from their exposure to respirable asbestos fibers and cigarette smoke. The plaintiffs allege that</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"> Mrs.&#160;Parsons&#8217; use of tobacco products and exposure to asbestos products caused her to develop lung cancer and to become addicted to tobacco. In December&#160;2000, three defendants, Nitral Liquidators, Inc., Desseaux Corporation of North America and Armstrong </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">World Industries, filed bankruptcy petitions in the U.S.&#160;Bankruptcy Court for the District of Delaware, </font><font style="font-style:italic;">In re Armstrong World Industries, Inc. </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">Pursuant to section&#160;362(a) of the Bankruptcy Code, </font><font style="font-style:italic;">Parsons </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">is automatically stayed with respect to all defendants</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"> who filed for bankruptcy. The case remains pending against the other defendants, including RJR Tobacco and Lorillard Tobacco, but it has long been dormant.</font></p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:4.54%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">Finally, in <font style="font-style:italic;">Jones v.&#160;American Tobacco Co., Inc., </font>a case filed in December 1998 in Circuit Court, Jackson County, Missouri, the defendants removed the case to the U.S.&#160;District Court for the Western District of Missouri in February&#160;1999. The action was brought against the major U.S.&#160;cigarette manufacturers, including RJR Tobacco, B&amp;W, Lorillard Tobacco, and parent companies of U.S.&#160;cigarette manufacturers, including RJR and Lorillard, by tobacco product users and purchasers on behalf of all similarly situated Missouri consumers. The plaintiffs allege that their use of the defendants&#8217; tobacco products has caused them to become addicted to nicotine. The plaintiffs seek to recover an unspecified amount of compensatory and punitive damages. The case was remanded to the Circuit Court in February&#160;1999. There is currently no activity in this case.</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:18pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:0%;font-style:italic;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"><a name="FILTER_CASES"></a><a name="FILTER_CASES"></a>Filter Cases</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:6pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:4.54%;color:#000000;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"><font style="Background-color:#FFFFFF;">Claims have been brought against Lorillard Tobacco and Lorillard by individuals who seek damages resulting from their alleged exposure to asbestos fibers that were incorporated into filter material used in one brand of cigarettes manufactured by a predecessor to Lorillard Tobacco for a limited period of time ending more than 50 years ago. As of December 31, 2015, Lorillard Tobacco and/or Lorillard was a defendant in 64 </font><font style="Background-color:#FFFFFF;">Filter</font><font style="Background-color:#FFFFFF;"> Cases. Since January&#160;1, 2012, Lorillard Tobacco has paid, or has reached agreement to pay, a total of approximately $51.8 million in settlements to resolve 187 claims asserted in Filter Cases. </font></p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:4.54%;color:#000000;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"><font style="Background-color:#FFFFFF;">Pursuant to the terms of a 1952 agreement between P. Lorillard Company and H&amp;V Specialties Co., Inc. (the manufacturer of the filter material), Lorillard Tobacco is required to indemnify Hollingsworth&#160;&amp; Vose for legal fees, expenses, judgments and resolutions in cases and claims alleging injury from finished products sold by P. Lorillard Company that contained the filter material. </font></p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:4.54%;color:#000000;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"><font style="Background-color:#FFFFFF;">On September&#160;13, 2013, the jury in </font><font style="font-style:italic;Background-color:#FFFFFF;">DeLisle v. A. W. Chesterton Company</font><font style="Background-color:#FFFFFF;">, a case tried in the Circuit Court for the 17<sup style="font-size:85%; vertical-align:top">th</sup> Judicial Circuit, Broward County, Florida, found in favor of the plaintiffs as to their claims for negligence and strict liability, and awarded $8 million. Lorillard Tobacco is responsible for 44%, or $3.52 million. Judgment was entered on November&#160;6, 2013. Lorillard Tobacco filed its notice of appeal on November&#160;18, 2013. </font><font style="color:#000000;">Briefing is complete. </font><font style="Background-color:#FFFFFF;">Oral argument is scheduled for February 16, 2016. </font></p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:18pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:0%;font-style:italic;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"><a name="HEALTHCARE_COST_RECOVERY_CASES"></a>Health-Care <a name="HEALTHCARE_COST_RECOVERY_CASES"></a>Cost Recovery Cases</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:6pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:4.54%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">Health-care cost recovery cases have been brought by a variety of plaintiffs. Other than certain governmental actions, these cases largely have been unsuccessful on remoteness grounds, which means that one who pays an injured person&#8217;s medical expenses is legally too remote to maintain an action against the person allegedly responsible for the injury.</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:4.54%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">As of December 31, 2015, two health-care cost recovery cases were pending in the United States against RJR Tobacco, B&amp;W, Lorillard Tobacco, or all three, as discussed below after the discussion of the State Settlement Agreements. A limited number of claimants have filed suit against RJR Tobacco, one of its affiliates, and other tobacco industry defendants to recover funds for health care, medical and other assistance paid by foreign provincial governments in treating their citizens. For additional information on these cases, see &#8220;&#8212; International Cases&#8221; below.</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:4.54%;font-style:italic;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">State Settlement Agreements.<font style="font-style:normal;"> In June 1994, the Mississippi Attorney General brought an action, </font>Moore&#160;v. American Tobacco Co.<font style="font-style:normal;">, against various industry members, including RJR Tobacco, B&amp;W and Lorillard Tobacco. This case was brought on behalf of the state to recover state funds paid for health care and other assistance to state citizens suffering from diseases and conditions allegedly related to tobacco use. Most other states, through their attorneys general or other state agencies, sued RJR Tobacco, B&amp;W, Lorillard Tobacco and other U.S.&#160;cigarette manufacturers based on similar theories. The cigarette manufacturer defendants, including RJR Tobacco, B&amp;W and Lorillard Tobacco, settled the first four of these cases scheduled for trial&#160;&#8212; Mississippi, Florida, Texas and Minnesota&#160;&#8212; by separate agreements with each such state.</font></p>
<p style="text-align:center;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:0%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">135</p>
<hr style="page-break-after:always;width:100%;">
<p style="text-align:center;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;text-indent:0%;font-weight:bold;font-family:Times New Roman Bold;font-size:10pt;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"><font style="Background-color:#FFFFFF;">NOTES TO CONSOLIDATED FINANCIAL STATEMENTS &#8212; continued</font></p>
<p style="margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;text-indent:0%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">&#160;</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:4.54%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">On November&#160;23, 1998,</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"> the major U.S.&#160;cigarette manufacturers, including RJR Tobacco</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">, B&amp;W</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"> and </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">Lorillard Tobacco</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">, entered into the Master Settlement Agreement with attorneys general representing the remaining 46&#160;states, the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico, Guam, the Virgin Isl</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">ands, American Samoa and the Northern Marianas. Effective on November&#160;12, 1999, the MSA settled all the health-care cost recovery actions brought by, or on behalf of, the settling jurisdictions and released various additional present and future claims.</font></p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:4.54%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">In the settling jurisdictions, the MSA released RJR Tobacco, B&amp;W, Lorillard Tobacco, and their affiliates and indemnitees, including RAI and Lorillard, from:</p>

<p style="border-bottom:Solid 1pt;padding-bottom:1pt;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;margin-right:83.33%;text-indent:0%;font-size:6pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">&#160;</p>
<div align="left">
<table border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0"  style="border-collapse:collapse; width:100%;">
<tr>
<td valign="top" style="width:3.4%;white-space:nowrap">
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;font-size:7.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"><font style="font-size:7.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"><sup style="font-size:85%; vertical-align:top">(2)</sup></font></p></td>
<td valign="top">
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:7.5pt;"><sup style="font-size:85%; vertical-align:top"></sup><font style="font-size:10pt;">Amounts beginning in 2013 reflect the impact of the Term Sheet described below under &#8220;&#8212; State Settlement Agreements &#8212; Enforcement and Validity; Adjustments &#8212; Partial Settlement of Certain NPM Adjustment Claims.&#8221; </font></p></td></tr></table></div>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:4.54%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">The State Settlement Agreements also contain provisions restricting the marketing of tobacco products. Among these provisions are restrictions or prohibitions on the use of cartoon characters, brand-name sponsorships, apparel and other merchandise, outdoor and transit advertising, payments for product placement, free sampling and lobbying. Furthermore, the State Settlement Agreements required the dissolution of three industry-sponsored research and trade organizations. </p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:4.54%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">The State Settlement Agreements have materially adversely affected RJR Tobacco&#8217;s shipment volumes. RAI believes that these settlement obligations may materially adversely affect the results of operations, cash flows or financial position of RAI and RJR Tobacco in future periods. The degree of the adverse impact will depend, among other things, on the rate of decline in U.S.&#160;cigarette sales in the premium and value categories, RJR Tobacco&#8217;s share of the domestic premium and value cigarette categories, and the effect of any resulting cost advantage of manufacturers not subject to the State Settlement Agreements.</p>
<p style="text-align:center;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:0%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">136</p>
<hr style="page-break-after:always;width:100%;">
<p style="text-align:center;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;text-indent:0%;font-weight:bold;font-family:Times New Roman Bold;font-size:10pt;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"><font style="Background-color:#FFFFFF;">NOTES TO CONSOLIDATED FINANCIAL STATEMENTS &#8212; continued</font></p>
<p style="margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;text-indent:0%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">&#160;</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:4.54%;font-style:italic;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"><font style="font-style:italic;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">U.S. Department of Justice Case.</font><font style="font-style:normal;"> On September&#160;22, 1999, in </font><font style="font-style:italic;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">United States v. Philip Morris USA Inc.,</font><font style="font-style:normal;"> the U.S.&#160;Department of Justice brought an action against RJR Tobacco, B&amp;W</font><font style="font-style:normal;">, Lorillard Tobacc</font><font style="font-style:normal;">o </font><font style="font-style:normal;">and other tobacco companies in the U.S.&#160;District Court for the District of Columbia. The government initially sought to recover federal funds expended by the federal government in providing health care to smokers who developed diseases and injuries alleg</font><font style="font-style:normal;">ed to be smoking-related, based on several federal statutes. In addition, the government sought, pursuant to the civil provisions of RICO, disgorgement of profits the government contends were earned as a consequence of a RICO racketeering &#8220;enterprise.&#8221; In </font><font style="font-style:normal;">September 2000, the</font><font style="font-style:normal;"> district</font><font style="font-style:normal;"> court dismissed the government&#8217;s claims asserted under the Medical Care Recovery Act as well as those under the Medicare Secondary Payer provisions of the Social Security Act, but did not dismiss the RICO claims. In February 20</font><font style="font-style:normal;">05, the </font><font style="font-style:normal;">D.C. Circuit </font><font style="font-style:normal;">ruled that disgorgement is not an available remedy in this case. The government&#8217;s petition for writ of certiorari with the U.S.&#160;Supreme Court was denied in October 2005. The non-jury, bench trial began in September 2004, and closing ar</font><font style="font-style:normal;">guments concluded in June&#160;2005.</font></p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:4.54%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">On August&#160;17, 2006, the district court found certain defendants, including RJR Tobacco, B&amp;W and Lorillard Tobacco had violated RICO, but did not impose any direct financial penalties. The district court instead enjoined RJR Tobacco, Lorillard Tobacco and the defendants from committing future racketeering acts, participating in certain trade organizations, making misrepresentations concerning smoking and health and youth marketing, and using certain brand descriptors such as &#8220;low tar,&#8221; &#8220;light,&#8221; &#8220;ultra light,&#8221; &#8220;mild&#8221; and &#8220;natural.&#8221; The district court also ordered RJR Tobacco, Lorillard Tobacco and the other defendants to issue &#8220;corrective communications&#8221; on five subjects, including smoking and health and addiction, and to comply with further undertakings, including maintaining web sites of historical corporate documents and disseminating certain marketing information on a confidential basis to the government. In addition, the district court placed restrictions on the defendants&#8217; ability to dispose of certain assets for use in the United States, unless the transferee agrees to abide by the terms of the district court&#8217;s order, and ordered certain defendants to reimburse the U.S.&#160;Department of Justice its taxable costs incurred in connection with the case.</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:4.54%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">Certain defendants, including RJR Tobacco and Lorillard Tobacco, filed notices of appeal to the D.C. Circuit in September&#160;2006. The government filed its notice of appeal in October&#160;2006. In addition, the defendants, including RJR Tobacco and Lorillard Tobacco, filed joint motions asking the district court to clarify and to stay its order pending the defendants&#8217; appeal. On September&#160;28, 2006, the district court denied the defendants&#8217; motion to stay. On September&#160;29, 2006, the defendants, including RJR Tobacco and Lorillard Tobacco, filed a motion asking the D.C. Circuit to stay the district court&#8217;s order pending the defendants&#8217; appeal. The D.C. Circuit granted the motion in October&#160;2006.</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:4.54%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">In November&#160;2006, the D.C. Circuit stayed the appeals pending the district court&#8217;s ruling on the defendants&#8217; motion for clarification. The defendants&#8217; motion was granted in part and denied in part. The defendants&#8217; motion as to the meaning and applicability of the general injunctive relief of the August&#160;2006 order was denied. The request for clarification as to the scope of the provisions in the order prohibiting the use of descriptors and requiring corrective statements at retail point of sale was granted. The district court also ruled that the provisions prohibiting the use of express or implied health messages or descriptors do apply to the actions of the defendants taken outside of the United States.</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:4.54%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">In May&#160;2009, the D.C. Circuit largely affirmed the finding of liability against the tobacco defendants and remanded to the trial court for dismissal of the trade organizations. The D.C. Circuit also largely affirmed the remedial order, including the denial of additional remedies, but vacated the order and remanded for further proceedings as to the following four discrete issues:</p>

In June 2010, the U.S. Supreme Court denied the parties&#8217; petitions for writ of certiorari. </p>
<p style="text-align:center;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:0%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">137</p>
